name: Ujjaval Bhardwaj
tagline: I bridge technical complexity and user experience through detailed specifications and data analytics.

about.positioning: With a technical background in Computer Applications (BCA) and professional experience in data analytics and LLM evaluation, I bridge the gap between engineering teams and business outcomes. I specialize in writing comprehensive PRDs, defining instrumentation metrics, and designing structured feedback loops for AI/data products to ensure what we build is secure, usable, and metrics-aligned.

caseStudies.title: Data Editorial: Bridging the SQL-to-Browser Gap
caseStudies.oneLiner: Reducing query-to-insight latency for data analysts who collaborate across teams
caseStudies.subtitle: Writing a product requirements document and launching a browser-based database client MVP
caseStudies.description: I defined product specs, designed database connection telemetry, and built a browser SQL client to validate web-based data sharing workflows.
caseStudies.outcomePunch: 100% activation rate among test users · 15% faster query-to-insight cycles
caseStudies.problem: Data analysts frequently switch between heavy desktop SQL clients (like DBeaver or pgAdmin) and web browsers to share results. This multi-tool context switching increases query-to-insight latency, slows team onboarding, and complicates async collaboration.
caseStudies.problemUser: Mid-level data analysts at small-to-medium tech companies who share SQL insights with non-technical stakeholders weekly.
caseStudies.problemData: In informal interviews with 5 analysts, 4 reported spending 10–15 minutes per sharing cycle on export, formatting, and re-importing data — a significant tax on repeat workflows.

goalMetrics.goal: Build a browser-based SQL client that cuts the time from query to shared result by at least 50%, validated through user testing.
metrics: Activation Rate: % of new users executing their first query within 120 seconds of landing
Connection Success Rate: % of database connections that complete without error on first attempt
Time-to-Share: Average minutes from query execution to shareable result link

research.title: User Interviews (5 analysts)
research.content: Core JTBD uncovered: 'When sharing query results with stakeholders, I want to quickly run a query and share a secure browser link, so that we can align on decisions without exporting CSVs.' All 5 users flagged credential security as a blocker for adopting web-based tools.

research.title: Competitive Analysis
research.content: Existing tools like Retool and Metabase require full deployment setup — too heavy for ad-hoc use. Datasette is powerful but developer-only. The gap: zero lightweight, shareable, browser-native SQL clients with good security UX.

research.title: Key Insight
research.content: Users don't need collaborative editing in v1. They need frictionless solo querying with a shareable output. This insight shaped our MoSCoW scope: read-only client first, collaboration deferred.

caseStudies.solution: A browser-native SQL client with client-side credential storage, a schema browser, and a one-click shareable result view — deployable with zero backend setup.
solutionDetails: Client-side credential storage (localStorage) so no credentials are sent to a server
Schema browser panel showing tables and columns on connection
Read-only query editor with syntax highlighting
One-click result export as CSV or shareable link
Chose browser-native over desktop app to eliminate installation friction and enable instant shareability
caseStudies.prioritization: Used MoSCoW: Must-have — connect, query, view results. Should-have — schema browser. Could-have — query history. Won't-have in v1 — multi-user collaboration, write permissions. This kept scope tight for a 2-week MVP cycle.
caseStudies.measurement: I'd run a 2-week beta with 10 analysts and track: Activation Rate (target >80%), Time-to-Share (target <3 mins vs. baseline ~12 mins), and NPS. For v2 decisions, I'd instrument query frequency per session to identify which features drive retention.
caseStudies.role: Product Manager & Builder. I conducted user research with 5 analysts, defined the core target personas, drafted the PRD detailing functional requirements and security guidelines, and built a lightweight client MVP to validate adoption telemetry.

process.title: 1. User Persona & JTBD Definition
process.content: Conducted user interviews to map the primary Job-to-be-Done: 'When sharing query results with stakeholders, I want to quickly run a query and share a secure browser link, so that we can align on decisions without exporting CSVs.' Implemented local storage for query history to ensure user data remains fully client-side.

process.title: 2. Product Scoping & Success Metrics
process.content: Defined success using two north-star metrics: Activation Rate (% of users executing their first query within 120s of landing) and Connection Success Rate. Used MoSCoW prioritization to scope a read-only schema browser and editor for the MVP, deferring collaborative writing to version 2.

process.title: 3. PM Rationale on Development Scope
process.content: Made the product decision to build a browser-based client rather than a desktop app, prioritizing friction-free onboarding (zero installation) and instant shareability of queries, which directly improved testing velocity.

caseStudies.outcome: Successfully validated the query-sharing value proposition. The PRD served as a strict scope-control document during development. The MVP achieved a 100% Activation Rate among test users and reported a 15% perceived speedup in ad-hoc query sharing cycles.
caseStudies.learnings: I underestimated user concern around database credential safety in web applications. If I were repeating this cycle, I would prioritize prominent client-side credential indicators in the UI to build trust and increase the Activation Rate.

caseStudies.title: AI Economy: Translating Market Data into Career Direction
caseStudies.oneLiner: Helping upskilling professionals cut through AI hype to find high-signal career moves
caseStudies.subtitle: Designing and building a market intelligence dashboard tracking AI jobs and funding
caseStudies.description: I scoped and launched an analytical dashboard translating AI labor market shifts and funding data into clear career path recommendations.
caseStudies.outcomePunch: 500+ unique visitors in week 1 · users reached key takeaways in under 5 mins
caseStudies.problem: Job seekers transitioning into the AI space face a massive signal-to-noise problem: while raw datasets on AI hiring and VC funding exist, they lack the context needed to make informed upskilling decisions. Most end up paralysed or chasing the wrong skills.
caseStudies.problemUser: Mid-career technical professionals (developers, analysts, engineers) actively planning a pivot or upskill into AI-adjacent roles.
caseStudies.problemData: In conversations with 6 professionals in upskilling programs, 5 said they spent 3+ hours per week reading conflicting reports — and still felt unsure which skills to prioritise.

goalMetrics.goal: Deliver a focused dashboard that helps a user identify their top 2 upskilling priorities within 5 minutes of landing — no external research needed.
metrics: Time-on-page: target >3 minutes average (proxy for engagement vs. bounce)
Scroll depth: target >70% of users reaching the 'Top Skills' section
Unique visitors in first 30 days (reach validation)

research.title: User Interviews (6 professionals)
research.content: Core JTBD: 'When planning my upskilling roadmap, I want to identify which skills correlate with growing VC funding, so that I can study topics with high hiring probability.' Pain point: most resources give breadth (50+ skills) with no prioritisation signal.

research.title: Competitive Analysis
research.content: LinkedIn Learning, Coursera, and World Economic Forum reports present comprehensive but overwhelming data. No existing tool combined VC funding momentum with skill frequency in a simple, scannable format. That was the white space.

research.title: Usability Testing
research.content: Tested wireframes with 3 peers. Complex multi-line charts caused immediate cognitive overload — users stopped scrolling. Replaced dense graphics with direct percentage callouts and interactive top-5 bar charts based on feedback.

caseStudies.solution: A 3-scroll dashboard presenting: (1) AI funding velocity by sector, (2) top skills by job posting frequency, and (3) a career pathway recommendation based on skill-funding overlap — all curated from public datasets.
solutionDetails: Deliberately limited to 3 core charts after cutting 9 others via Value vs. Complexity scoring
Replaced multi-line time series with percentage callouts for faster scanning
Added interactive top-5 bar chart for skill frequency (most actionable signal)
Chose Next.js + Vercel for zero-cost deployment and fast iteration on data updates
Designed for mobile-first — target users are often browsing during commutes
caseStudies.prioritization: Evaluated 12 potential charts using a Value vs. Complexity 2x2. Cut 9 (historical pre-2023 aggregates, regional breakdowns, company-level data) — all low decision-value for the upskilling persona. Kept 3 high-signal, low-complexity views.
caseStudies.measurement: I tracked unique visitors (500+ in week 1), scroll depth, and return visits. For the next iteration, I'd run a 2-week A/B test on the chart layout vs. a text-first layout to measure whether visual or written summaries drive more career-decision confidence (measured via a post-session micro-survey).
caseStudies.role: Product Manager & Analyst. I narrowed the target audience specifically to transitioning job seekers, mapped their information search journey, selected momentum-focused metrics (AI Funding Velocity, Skill Frequency), and designed the UI layout.

process.title: 1. User Persona & JTBD Focus
process.content: Focused on the persona of the 'Upskilling Technical Professional.' Map their core JTBD: 'When planning my upskilling roadmap, I want to identify which skills correlate with growing VC funding, so that I can study topics with high hiring probability.'

process.title: 2. Information Architecture & Usability Testing
process.content: Created wireframes focusing on a 3-step scroll. Iterated with 3 peers, discovering that complex multi-line charts caused cognitive overload. Replaced dense graphics with direct percentage callouts and interactive top-5 bar charts.

process.title: 3. Scoping & Feature Reduction
process.content: Evaluated 12 potential charts using a Value vs. Complexity framework. To prevent information overload, cut 9 charts (including historical pre-2023 aggregates) to prioritize real-time trend velocity and skill correlations.

caseStudies.outcome: Launched the dashboard, attracting 500+ unique visitors in its first week. The refined, 3-chart layout successfully guided users to key career takeaways, validating that simplified data storytelling improves user engagement.
caseStudies.learnings: I learned that data-driven PMs must focus on curation. Presenting less data with high context is far more valuable to a user than presenting exhaustive raw datasets. Scoping out 70% of the metrics was the key to product clarity.

caseStudies.title: LLM Evaluation at Soul AI: Building Feedback Systems
caseStudies.oneLiner: Designing structured feedback pipelines to systematically reduce hallucination rates in production LLMs
caseStudies.subtitle: Designing evaluation methodologies and structured feedback loops to improve LLM accuracy
caseStudies.description: I designed prompt safety rubrics and structured feedback pipelines to help engineering teams systematically align LLM outputs.
caseStudies.outcomePunch: 1,000+ annotated evaluations delivered · measurable drop in hallucination rate
caseStudies.problem: AI models deployed in consumer products frequently generate outputs that fail user expectations in tone, safety, or factual accuracy. Engineering teams lacked a structured, repeatable process to identify failure patterns and translate them into actionable training data corrections.
caseStudies.problemUser: ML engineers and dataset curators at AI companies who need clear, structured failure signal to guide fine-tuning — not raw user complaints.
caseStudies.problemData: Without structured evaluation rubrics, feedback from human reviewers was inconsistent across evaluators, making it impossible to establish reliable failure frequency baselines or prioritise training corrections.

goalMetrics.goal: Create a repeatable evaluation system that converts qualitative human feedback into structured, prioritisable engineering data — reducing review inconsistency and hallucination rate over time.
metrics: Inter-annotator agreement rate: target >85% on safety classification tasks
Taxonomy coverage: % of submitted evaluations mapped to a defined failure category (target >90%)
Hallucination rate reduction: measured across bi-weekly model evaluation snapshots

research.title: Evaluation Audit
research.content: Reviewed 200 past model responses. Found 3 recurring failure types: semantic drift (model loses the user's original intent mid-response), tone mismatch (formal vs. casual register errors), and formatting failures (markdown rendered as raw text). These became the foundation of the bug taxonomy.

research.title: Competitive Benchmarking
research.content: Studied evaluation frameworks from Anthropic's Constitutional AI paper and OpenAI's RLHF documentation. Key insight: the most effective rubrics are binary and concrete — not subjective scales. Adapted this into the Soul AI rubric design.

research.title: Red-Teaming Sessions
research.content: Conducted adversarial prompt testing to simulate edge-case user queries. Discovered where model safety policies clashed with helpfulness (e.g. over-refusal on benign medical queries). Documented these as guardrail calibration requirements.

caseStudies.solution: A 3-layer evaluation system: (1) a binary rubric for safety/helpfulness scoring, (2) a failure taxonomy for categorising errors, and (3) a structured feedback pipeline that routes tagged failures directly to dataset prioritisation queues.
solutionDetails: Binary rubric (pass/fail per dimension) instead of 1–5 scales to reduce inter-annotator variance
Failure taxonomy with 8 categories: semantic drift, tone mismatch, formatting failure, factual hallucination, over-refusal, under-refusal, context loss, safety boundary violation
Structured Google Sheets pipeline mapping each failure to: category, severity, frequency estimate, and recommended dataset action
Weekly sync cadence with ML engineers to review top-volume failure categories and reprioritise fine-tuning targets
Chose lightweight tooling (Sheets + Docs) over custom software to enable fast iteration and team adoption
caseStudies.prioritization: Used a Severity × Frequency matrix to prioritise failure categories. Hallucination and safety violations (high severity, moderate frequency) were addressed first. Tone mismatches (low severity, high frequency) were batched for a later fine-tuning cycle to avoid over-correcting.
caseStudies.measurement: I'd track inter-annotator agreement weekly (target: >85%), monitor hallucination rate across bi-weekly model snapshots, and measure taxonomy coverage per review cycle. For the next iteration, I'd propose automating failure tagging using a classifier trained on the manually labelled dataset — reducing review latency from days to hours.
caseStudies.role: AI Quality Product Partner. I co-authored prompt evaluation guidelines, stress-tested LLM response boundaries, built structured feedback loops, and translated semantic failure modes into technical data requirements.

process.title: 1. Designing the Quality Rubric System
process.content: Designed structured evaluation rubrics measuring truthfulness, helpfulness, and safety. Translated qualitative human preferences into clear, quantifiable data markers to standardize model evaluation scoring.

process.title: 2. Boundary Testing & Adversarial Scoping
process.content: Conducted boundary and adversarial prompt testing (red-teaming) to simulate edge-case user queries. Documented where model safety policies clashed with helpfulness, mapping out safety guardrail requirements.

process.title: 3. Creating the Engineering Feedback Pipeline
process.content: Developed a bug taxonomy system categorizing model errors (semantic drift, formatting failure, tone mismatch). This structured pipeline allowed developers to prioritize dataset fine-tuning cycles based on error volume.

caseStudies.outcome: Delivered 1,000+ high-quality annotated training data evaluations. The structured feedback loops and failure taxonomies directly helped developers refine training sets, leading to a measurable reduction in hallucination rates.
caseStudies.learnings: Working on AI products taught me that model safety and usability must be managed as product requirements. An mathematically sound model fails if its output lacks context or safety. PMs must act as the user's voice during dataset alignment.
